title: Given the head of a singly linked list, determine whether the list has a cycle, meaning some node's next pointer points back to an earlier node. Solve it with constant extra space. (LeetCode: Linked List Cycle)
shortTitle: LinkedList Cycle (Floyd's Tortoise and Hare Detection)

s1_definition.profdef: Cycle detection in a linked list uses Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm: two pointers advance through the list at different speeds, one moving one node per step and the other two nodes per step. If the list has a cycle, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet; if the fast pointer reaches the end, there is no cycle. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh is following a chain of linked transaction records, each pointing to the next. Normally the chain ends, but a corruption bug can make a record point back to an earlier one, creating an endless loop. To detect this without writing down every record he has seen, he sends two readers down the chain: a slow reader moving one record at a time and a fast reader moving two at a time. If the chain loops, the fast reader keeps circling and eventually catches up to the slow reader from behind. If the fast reader hits the end, the chain is clean.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two walkers at different speeds; if they ever meet, there is a loop; if the fast one hits the end, there is not.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Cycle detection in a linked list uses Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm: two pointers advance through the list at different speeds, one moving one node per step and the other two nodes per step. If the list has a cycle, the fast pointer eventually laps the slow pointer and they meet; if the fast pointer reaches the end, there is no cycle. This runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh is following a chain of linked transaction records, each pointing to the next. Normally the chain ends, but a corruption bug can make a record point back to an earlier one, creating an endless loop. To detect this without writing down every record he has seen, he sends two readers down the chain: a slow reader moving one record at a time and a fast reader moving two at a time. If the chain loops, the fast reader keeps circling and eventually catches up to the slow reader from behind. If the fast reader hits the end, the chain is clean.

**One line to remember:** Two walkers at different speeds; if they ever meet, there is a loop; if the fast one hits the end, there is not.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach stores every node it visits in a hash set and checks each new node against the set; if a node repeats, there is a cycle. That works but uses extra space proportional to the list length. Floyd's algorithm achieves the same result with just two pointers and no extra storage.

We start both a `slow` and a `fast` pointer at the head. In each iteration we move `slow` forward by one node and `fast` forward by two nodes. If at any point `fast` or `fast.next` becomes null, the list has an end, so there is no cycle and we return false. If `slow` and `fast` ever point to the same node, they have met inside a loop, so there is a cycle and we return true.

The reason this works is a simple relative-speed argument. If there is a cycle, once both pointers are inside it, the fast pointer gains one node of distance on the slow pointer every step. Because the loop has a fixed number of nodes, that gap closes and the fast pointer lands exactly on the slow pointer; it cannot jump over it, because the gap shrinks by exactly one each step. If there is no cycle, the fast pointer simply runs off the end.

A finance usage example: suppose a chain of transaction records is `T1 -> T2 -> T3 -> T4 -> T2`, where T4 wrongly points back to T2. The slow pointer visits T1, T2, T3, and the fast pointer visits T1, T3, T2, T4, and so on; inside the loop the fast pointer catches the slow one, confirming the corruption.

The senior-level nuance: the loop condition must check both `fast` and `fast.next` for null before advancing two steps, otherwise a null dereference occurs on an even-length acyclic list. The hash-set method is sometimes acceptable and even preferable when you also need to know which nodes form the cycle, but when the interviewer emphasizes constant space, Floyd's algorithm is the expected answer. This same two-speed idea extends to finding the start of the cycle and the cycle's length.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India links related transaction records into a chain where each record points to the next in a logical sequence. A rare data-corruption bug can cause one record to point back to an earlier record, creating an infinite loop that hangs any process that walks the chain. The integrity checker must detect such a loop before downstream processing, and it must do so without storing every visited record, because the chains can be enormous.

Problem 2 — The checker runs on memory-constrained infrastructure and must use constant extra space regardless of chain length, which rules out the hash-set approach and points to Floyd's two-pointer method.

The code defines a `ChainIntegrityChecker` class with a `hasCycle` method implementing the tortoise and hare. A runnable demo builds both a clean chain and a corrupted looping chain and logs whether each has a cycle.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: first a clean chain `T1 -> T2 -> T3 -> T4 -> null`, then a corrupted chain where T4 points back to T2.

Step 1: For the clean chain, both slow and fast start at T1. The loop checks that fast and fast.next are not null, which is true.

Step 2: Slow moves to T2 and fast moves to T3. They are not equal. The loop checks again: fast is T3, fast.next is T4, not null.

Step 3: Slow moves to T3 and fast moves two steps, landing past T4 at null. The loop condition now sees fast is null, so it exits and the method returns false. The clean chain has no cycle.

Step 4: For the corrupted chain, T4 points back to T2, so the chain loops among T2, T3, T4. Both pointers start at T1.

Step 5: Slow advances one and fast advances two each iteration. Inside the loop the fast pointer gains one node per step on the slow pointer, the gap closes, and eventually slow and fast land on the same node. The method logs a severe message and returns true, confirming the corruption.

Final output:

```
Oct 27, 2026 6:45:00 PM com.bank.integrity.ChainIntegrityDemo main
INFO: No cycle; chain is clean.
INFO: Clean chain has cycle: false
SEVERE: Cycle detected in transaction chain.
INFO: Corrupted chain has cycle: true
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Detecting a cycle in a singly linked list is the classic use of Floyd's tortoise and hare algorithm, which finds a loop in linear time using only two pointers and no extra storage. The naive alternative records every node it visits in a hash set and checks for a repeat, but that uses space proportional to the list length, whereas Floyd's method uses constant space.

I start a slow pointer and a fast pointer at the head. On each step the slow pointer moves forward one node and the fast pointer moves forward two nodes. If the fast pointer or its next ever becomes null, the list has a genuine end, so there is no cycle and I return false. If the slow and fast pointers ever land on the same node, they have met inside a loop, so a cycle exists and I return true. The reason they are guaranteed to meet when there is a cycle is a relative-speed argument: once both are inside the loop, the fast pointer closes the gap to the slow pointer by exactly one node every step, so the gap shrinks to zero and the fast pointer lands precisely on the slow one without ever jumping over it.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in an integrity checker. We linked related transaction records into a chain where each record pointed to the next, and a rare corruption bug could make a record point back to an earlier one, creating an infinite loop that would hang any process walking the chain. The chains could be enormous and the checker ran on memory-constrained infrastructure, so storing every visited record was not acceptable, and the two-pointer method detected the corruption safely in constant space before downstream processing.

The senior-level point I stress is the null safety in the loop condition. Before advancing the fast pointer two steps I must check that both the fast pointer and its next are non-null, otherwise an even-length acyclic list causes a null dereference. I also note that the hash-set approach is a reasonable choice when I additionally need to identify which specific nodes form the cycle, but when constant space is the priority, Floyd's algorithm is the right tool, and the same two-speed idea extends naturally to finding where the cycle begins and how long it is.
